paras: The threatened lynching of Alfred Lewis took place at Barnum, Minnesota, in March 1888, after Lewis, a Black restaurant keeper, was jailed on an accusation of killing Frank Burke. The St. Paul Daily Globe reported the threat but described no crowd or attempt, and a week later found Lewis still in jail, claiming self-defense.

Lewis, described as "an inoffensive-looking mulatto, apparently about forty years of age," had lived in Duluth from 1865 to 1885 before keeping a restaurant at Barnum. Burke, a section hand on the St. Paul & Duluth road, was a stranger in the town.

According to the Globe's first report, Burke came to the restaurant after drinking at the Barnum saloon, was refused a bed, became quarrelsome and fought Lewis. He was found dead outdoors the next morning with a fractured skull, and bystanders said Lewis "must have used something besides his fists." An official at Northern Pacific Junction, whose name is cut off in the surviving text, reported that Burke died by "a blow from a blunt instrument in the hands of" Lewis.

Lewis was arrested and jailed, and the report closed with the sentence "Lewis is threatened with lynching." It did not say who made the threat, and no crowd or attempt on Lewis appears in the coverage.
A Duluth dispatch of 21 March, naming him Albert Lewis and dating the killing to 12 March, placed him in the county jail. No report of an indictment, trial or verdict was found.

The episode appears only in the Duluth column of the St. Paul Daily Globe, on 14 and 22 March 1888. The first headline called Lewis "THE MURDERER" and gave the threat one closing line, without comment. The follow-up shifted to "Accused of Murder," gave Lewis's version at length and did not mention the threat.

The two reports differ on how Burke died: the first, resting on an official report and bystanders, blamed a blunt instrument. Lewis said Burke attacked him, that he struck back with a pine stick in self-defense, and that Burke was hurt in a fall after leaving.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Alfred Lewis
bases: The only mob element is the single statement that Lewis, a jailed Black man accused of killing a stranger, 'is threatened with lynching' (A1); no crowd, attack on the jail or other act is reported (A1, A2).
Lewis was not killed: a week after the threat he was reported alive in the county jail (A2); the threat itself is one sentence naming no group, size or act (A1).
Both reports are Duluth correspondence in the St. Paul Daily Globe; the jailing and Burke's death appear in both, but the lynching threat appears only in A1 and is not repeated in A2.

accounts.label: Official report and bystanders
accounts.gist: Burke, drunk and refused a bed, became quarrelsome and fought Lewis; bystanders said Lewis 'must have used something besides his fists,' and Burke was found dead outdoors the next morning with a fractured skull.

accounts.label: Lewis's account
accounts.gist: Burke insisted on a room, became violent and attacked him; Lewis struck him several times with a pine stick in self-defense, did not think the blows fatal, and believed Burke fell and was hurt after leaving.

framing.detail: The Globe's first report headlined Lewis as 'THE MURDERER' and mentioned the lynching threat in a closing sentence without comment.
The follow-up called Lewis 'Accused of Murder' and 'inoffensive-looking,' gave his self-defense account at length and did not mention the threat.

conflicts.note: Same paper, same Duluth column; both place him at Barnum and accuse him of killing Frank Burke.

versions.value: A blow from a blunt instrument in Lewis's hands; bystanders said Lewis used more than his fists; skull fractured before or while he was thrown out
Lewis struck him with a pine stick in self-defense after Burke attacked; Burke probably fell and was hurt after leaving

conflicts.note: A1 rests on the official report and bystanders; A2 is Lewis's own account. Both agree on a fight after Burke was refused a room.

Alfred Lewis (A1), called Albert Lewis (A2), a 'colored' restaurant keeper at Barnum (A1), 'an inoffensive-looking mulatto, apparently about forty' (A2); threatened, not harmed
